danish.title: Tiende bog (1812) — Kapitel 34
paragraphs: Napoleons generaler — Davout, Ney og Murat, der var tæt på ildzonen og til tider selv gik ind i den — førte gentagne gange vældige masser af velordnede tropper derind. Men i modsætning til, hvad der altid var sket ved deres tidligere slag, kom der i stedet for nyheder om fjendens flugt kun ordnede tropper tilbage i vild uorden. De førte dem frem igen, men hver gang var der færre af dem, der vendte tilbage.
Napoleon sad ved foden af bakken og drak punsch, da Murats adjudant kom i galop med en forsikring om, at russerne ville blive slået, hvis Hans Majestæt ville give ham endnu en division.

»Forstærkninger?« sagde Napoleon i en tone af streng overraskelse og kiggede på adjudanten — en smuk ung mand med langt, sort krøllet hår arrangeret ligesom Murats eget — som om han ikke forstod hans ord.
»Forstærkninger!« tænkte Napoleon for sig selv. »Hvordan kan de have brug for forstærkninger, når de allerede har halvdelen af hæren rettet mod en svag, ubefæstet russisk fløj?«
»Sig til Kongen af Napoli,« sagde han strengt, »at klokken endnu ikke er tolv, og at jeg endnu ikke kan se skakbrættet klart. Gå!...«
Den smukke unge adjudant med det lange hår sukkede dybt uden at tage hånden fra sin hue og galoperede tilbage til det sted, hvor mennesker blev slagtet.
Napoleon rejste sig og tilkaldte Caulaincourt og Berthier og begyndte at tale med dem om ting, der intet havde med slaget at gøre.

Midt i denne samtale, der begyndte at fange Napoleons interesse, vendte Berthiers blik mod en general med følge, der i galop red mod bakken på en skummende hest. Det var Belliard. Lige dér steg han af og gik med hurtige skridt hen til kejseren og begyndte dristigt at fremlægge nødvendigheden af at sende forstærkninger. Han svor på sin ære, at russerne var fortabte, hvis kejseren ville give endnu en division.
Napoleon trak på skuldrene og fortsatte med at gå frem og tilbage uden at svare. Belliard begyndte at tale højt og ivrigt med generalerne i følget.
»De er meget hidsig, Belliard,« sagde Napoleon, da han igen kom hen til generalen. »I kampens hede er det let at tage fejl. Gå hen og se en gang til, og kom så tilbage til mig.«
Før Belliard var ude af syne, kom en budbringer fra en anden del af slagmarken galoperende.
»Nå, hvad vil De?« spurgte Napoleon i den tone, en mand bruger, der er irriteret over hele tiden at blive forstyrret.
»Sire, fyrsten...« begyndte adjudanten.
»Beder om forstærkninger?« sagde Napoleon med en vred gestus.
Adjudanten nikkede bekræftende og begyndte at rapportere, men kejseren vendte sig fra ham, tog et par skridt, standsede, kom tilbage og kaldte på Berthier.
»Vi må give reserver,« sagde han og spredte armene en smule. »Hvem synes De, vi skal sende derhen?« spurgte han Berthier (som han senere betegnede som »den gåseunge, jeg har gjort til en ørn«).
»Send Claparèdes division, Sire,« svarede Berthier, der kendte alle divisioner, regimenter og bataljoner udenad.
Napoleon nikkede samtykke.
Adjudanten galoperede til Claparèdes division, og få minutter senere rykkede Den Unge Garde, der stod bag bakken, fremad. Napoleon kiggede tavst i den retning.
»Nej!« sagde han pludselig til Berthier. »Jeg kan ikke sende Claparède. Send Friants division.«

Selvom der ikke var nogen fordel i at sende Friants division i stedet for Claparèdes — ja, der var endda en åbenlys ulempe og forsinkelse i at standse Claparède og sende Friant nu — blev ordren udført til punkt og prikke. Napoleon opdagede ikke, at han i forholdet til sin hær spillede rollen som en læge, der er til gene med sin medicin — en rolle, han så klart havde udpeget og fordømt.

Friants division forsvandt i slagmarkens røg ligesom de andre. Fra alle sider kom adjudanter fortsat galoperende, og som efter aftale sagde de alle det samme. De bad alle om forstærkninger og sagde alle, at russerne holdt deres stillinger og opretholdt en frygtindgydende ild (un feu d'enfer), der fik de franske tropper til at smelte bort.
Napoleon sad på en feltstol, hensunket i tanker.
Monsieur de Beausset, manden der var så glad for at rejse, og som havde fastet siden morgen, kom hen til kejseren og vovede ærbødigt at foreslå Hans Majestæt frokost.
»Jeg håber, at jeg nu kan lykønske Deres Majestæt med en sejr?« sagde han.

Napoleon rystede tavst på hovedet. Da de Beausset antog, at afvisningen kun gjaldt sejren og ikke frokosten, vovede han med respektfuld skæmtsomhed at bemærke, at der ikke er nogen grund til at undlade at spise frokost, når man kan få den.
»Gå væk...« udbrød Napoleon pludselig og mut og vendte sig bort.
Et saligt smil af beklagelse, anger og henrykkelse strålede i monsieur de Beaussets ansigt, og han gled hen til de andre generaler.

Napoleon oplevede en følelse af depression som den, en altid heldig spiller føler, der efter hensynsløst at have kastet penge om sig og altid vundet, pludselig opdager — netop da han har beregnet alle spillets chancer — at jo mere han overvejer sit spil, desto sikrere taber han.

Hans tropper var de samme, hans generaler de samme, de samme forberedelser var truffet, den samme disposition og den samme proklamation — courte et énergique — han selv var stadig den samme: det vidste han, og han vidste, at han nu var endnu mere erfaren og dygtig end før. Selv fjenden var den samme som ved Austerlitz og Friedland. Men det frygtelige sving af armen, der havde virket vidunderligt stærkt, faldt nu slapt og magtesløst ned.

Alle de gamle metoder, der altid var blevet kronet med sejr — samlingen af batterier på ét punkt, et angreb med reserver for at bryde fjendens linje, et kavalerifremstød af »jernmændene« — alle disse metoder var allerede blevet anvendt, og dog var der ikke blot ingen sejr, men fra alle sider kom de samme meldinger om dræbte og sårede generaler, om at forstærkninger var nødvendige, om at russerne ikke kunne drives bort, og om at de franske tropper var i opløsning.

Tidligere — efter at han havde givet to-tre ordrer og sagt et par sætninger — var marskalker og adjudanter kommet galoperende med lykønskninger og glade ansigter, med meldinger om erobrede trofæer, om fangne korps, om bundter af fjendtlige ørne og faner, om kanoner og forsyninger, og Murat havde kun bedt om lov til at sætte kavaleriet ind for at opsamle bagagetrænet. Sådan var det gået ved Lodi, Marengo, Arcole, Jena, Austerlitz, Wagram og så videre. Men nu skete der noget mærkeligt med hans tropper.

Trods meldingen om erobringen af flècherne indså Napoleon, at dette ikke var det samme, slet ikke det samme som det, der var sket i hans tidligere slag. Han så, at det, han følte, blev følt af alle mændene omkring ham, erfarne som de var i krigskunsten. Alles ansigter så nedtrykte ud, og de undgik alle hinandens blik. Kun de Beausset forstod ikke, hvad der foregik.

Men Napoleon vidste med sin lange krigserfaring godt, hvad det betød, at et slag ikke var vundet af den angribende part efter otte timers indsats. Han vidste, at det var et tabt slag, og at den mindste tilfældighed nu — med kampen balancerende på en så anspændt knivsæg — kunne ødelægge ham og hans hær.

Da han i tankerne gennemgik hele dette mærkelige russiske felttog, hvor ikke ét slag var vundet, ikke en fane, en kanon eller et armékorps var erobret i to måneder — da han kiggede på de skjult nedtrykte ansigter omkring sig og hørte meldinger om, at russerne stadig holdt stand — overvældede ham en uhyggelig følelse, ligesom man oplever i onde drømme, og alle de uheldige tilfælde, der kunne ødelægge ham, meldte sig i hans tanker. Russerne kunne angribe hans venstre fløj, kunne gennembryde hans centrum, en vildfarent kanonkugle kunne dræbe ham selv. Alt dette var muligt. I hans tidligere slag havde han kun overvejet chancerne for held; nu fremstillede sig en uendelig række ulykkelige muligheder, og han ventede dem alle. Ja, det var som en ond drøm, hvor man ser en truende skikkelse nærme sig, svinger voldsomt for at slå den ned og mærker, at armen falder slapt og blødt som en klud — og rædslen ved hjælpeløsheden griber en.

Meldingen om, at russerne angreb den franske hærs venstre fløj, vakte netop den rædsel i Napoleon. Han sad tavst på en feltstol under bakken med bøjet hoved og albuerne på knæene. Berthier kom hen og foreslog, at de skulle ride langs linjen for at klarlægge situationen.
»Hvad? Hvad siger De?« spurgte Napoleon. »Ja, bed dem bringe mig min hest.«
Han steg til hest og red mod Semjonovsk.

I krudtrøgen, der langsomt lettede over hele det område, Napoleon red igennem, lå heste og mennesker i blodpøle, enkeltvis eller i dynger. Hverken Napoleon eller nogen af hans generaler havde før set sådanne rædsler eller så mange dræbte på så lille et stykke jord. I ti timer havde kanonerne brølet uden ophør. Drønene trættede øret og gav synet en egen betydning, som musikken gør det ved et levende tableau. Napoleon red op på højderne ved Semjonovskoje. Gennem røgen så han geledder af mænd i uniformer, hvis farve han ikke kendte. Det var russere.

Russerne stod i tætte rækker bag Semjonovsk og dens bakke, og deres kanoner drønede uafbrudt langs hele linjen og sendte røgskyer op. Det var ikke længere et slag: det var en vedvarende massakre, der hverken kunne gavne franskmænd eller russere. Napoleon standsede sin hest og faldt igen i de eftertanker, Berthier havde revet ham ud af; han kunne ikke standse det, der foregik for hans øjne og omkring ham, og som blev tilskrevet ham og afhang af hans vilje, men som for første gang — på grund af dets fejlslagne udfald — forekom ham unødvendigt og rædselsfuldt.

En af generalerne red hen til Napoleon og vovede at tilbyde at føre Den Gamle Garde i kamp. Ney og Berthier, der stod ved Napoleons side, udvekslede blikke og smilede foragteligt ad denne generals tåbelige tilbud.
Napoleon bøjede hovedet og sad længe tavs.
»Otte hundrede mil fra Frankrig vil jeg ikke lade min Garde blive ødelagt!« sagde han og vendte sin hest og red tilbage mod Sjevardino.

english.title: Book Ten (1812) — Chapter 34
paragraphs: Napoleon's generals — Davout, Ney, and Murat — who were near the zone of fire and sometimes even entered it, repeatedly led huge masses of well-organized troops into the fight. But contrary to what had always happened in their previous battles, instead of news of the enemy's retreat, these orderly formations came back as disorganized, terrified mobs. The generals re-formed them, but their numbers kept shrinking. In the middle of the day, Murat sent his adjutant to Napoleon demanding reinforcements.
Napoleon was sitting at the foot of the knoll, drinking punch, when Murat's adjutant galloped up assuring him that the Russians would be routed if His Majesty would provide one more division.
"Reinforcements?" said Napoleon in a tone of stern surprise, looking at the adjutant — a handsome young man with long black curls arranged like Murat's own — as though he didn't understand the words.
"Reinforcements!" Napoleon thought to himself. "How can they need reinforcements when they already have half the army directed against a weak, unfortified Russian flank?"
"Tell the King of Naples," he said sternly, "that it is not yet noon and I still don't see my chessboard clearly. Go!"
The handsome young adjutant with the long hair sighed deeply without removing his hand from his hat and galloped back to where men were being slaughtered.
Napoleon rose and, summoning Caulaincourt and Berthier, began talking to them about matters unrelated to the battle.

In the middle of this conversation, which was beginning to interest Napoleon, Berthier's eyes turned toward a general with a retinue galloping up the knoll on a lathered horse. It was Belliard. Dismounting, he strode rapidly up to the Emperor and in a loud voice began forcefully arguing the need for reinforcements. He swore on his honor that the Russians were finished if the Emperor would send one more division.
Napoleon shrugged and continued pacing without replying. Belliard began speaking loudly and urgently to the generals gathered around him.
"You are very excitable, Belliard," said Napoleon when he came up to the general again. "In the heat of battle it's easy to make mistakes. Go and have another look, then come back to me."
Before Belliard was out of sight, a messenger from another part of the battlefield galloped up.
"Well, what do you want?" Napoleon asked in the tone of a man irritated at being constantly interrupted.
"Sire, the prince..." the adjutant began.
"Wants reinforcements?" Napoleon said with an angry gesture.
The adjutant nodded and began to report, but the Emperor turned away, took a couple of steps, stopped, came back, and called Berthier.
"We need to commit the reserves," he said, spreading his arms slightly. "Who do you think should be sent?" he asked Berthier, whom he would later call "that gosling I turned into an eagle."
"Send Claparede's division, sire," replied Berthier, who knew every division, regiment, and battalion by heart.
Napoleon nodded in agreement.
The adjutant galloped off to Claparede's division, and a few minutes later the Young Guard, stationed behind the knoll, moved forward. Napoleon watched them silently.
"No!" he suddenly said to Berthier. "I can't send Claparede. Send Friant's division."

Though there was no advantage in sending Friant's division instead of Claparede's — and even an obvious inconvenience and delay in stopping Claparede and dispatching Friant now — the order was executed precisely. Napoleon didn't notice that with his army he was playing the role of the doctor who interferes with his medicines — a role he had so rightly understood and condemned in theory.

Friant's division vanished into the smoke like all the others. From every direction adjutants kept galloping up, and as if by agreement they all said the same thing: they all demanded reinforcements and reported that the Russians were holding their positions and maintaining a hellish fire under which the French army was melting away.
Napoleon sat on a camp stool, lost in thought.
Monsieur de Beausset, the man so fond of travel, having fasted since morning, approached the Emperor and respectfully ventured to suggest lunch to His Majesty.
"I hope I may now congratulate Your Majesty on a victory?" he said.

Napoleon silently shook his head. Assuming the refusal referred only to the victory and not to lunch, Monsieur de Beausset respectfully and playfully observed that there was no reason to skip a meal just because one couldn't get one.
"Go away!" Napoleon exclaimed suddenly and sourly, turning aside.
A blissful smile of regret, repentance, and rapture spread over Monsieur de Beausset's face, and he glided away to join the other generals.

Napoleon was experiencing a depression like that of a perpetually lucky gambler who, after recklessly throwing money around and always winning, suddenly finds — just when he has calculated all the odds — that the more carefully he plays, the more surely he loses.

His troops were the same, his generals the same, the same preparations had been made, the same formations set, and the same brief, forceful proclamation issued. He himself was still the same — he knew it, and knew he was now even more experienced and skilled than before. Even the enemy was the same as at Austerlitz and Friedland — yet the terrible stroke of his arm had somehow supernaturally become powerless.

All the old methods that had always been crowned with success — concentrating batteries on one point, attacking with reserves to break the enemy line, cavalry charges by his "men of iron" — all had been employed. Yet not only was there no victory, but from every direction came the same news: generals killed and wounded, reinforcements needed, the impossibility of driving back the Russians, and disorganization in his own troops.

In the past, after giving two or three orders and uttering a few phrases, marshals and adjutants would gallop up with congratulations and happy faces, announcing captured trophies, columns of prisoners, bundles of enemy flags and standards, cannons and supplies, while Murat only begged permission to unleash the cavalry to sweep up the baggage trains. So it had been at Lodi, Marengo, Arcola, Jena, Austerlitz, Wagram, and elsewhere. But now something strange was happening to his troops.

Despite reports of capturing the fortifications, Napoleon sensed that this was not the same — not at all the same — as his previous battles. He saw that what he was feeling was felt by all the experienced men around him. All their faces looked dejected, and they avoided each other's eyes — only a de Beausset could fail to grasp the meaning of what was happening.

But Napoleon, with his long experience of war, knew very well what it meant when the attacking side fails to win a battle after eight hours and all its efforts have been spent. He knew this was a lost battle, and that the slightest mishap — with things balanced on such a knife's edge — could destroy him and his army.

When he surveyed this entire strange Russian campaign, in which not a single battle had been won and not a flag, cannon, or army corps captured in two months; when he looked at the barely concealed despair on the faces around him and heard that the Russians were still holding their ground — a terrible feeling like a nightmare seized him, and every possible disaster that could destroy him flooded his mind. The Russians might fall on his left flank, might break through his center; he himself might be killed by a stray cannonball. All this was possible. In his previous battles he had only considered the possibilities of success, but now countless unlucky chances presented themselves, and he expected them all. Yes, it was like a dream where a man imagines a thug is coming to attack him, and he raises his arm to strike a terrible blow that should annihilate the attacker — only to feel his arm go limp and powerless like a rag, and the horror of inescapable destruction seizes him in his helplessness.

The news that the Russians were attacking the left flank of the French army aroused exactly that horror in Napoleon. He sat silently on a camp stool below the knoll, his head bowed, elbows on his knees. Berthier approached and suggested they ride along the line to assess the situation.
"What? What did you say?" Napoleon asked. "Yes, tell them to bring my horse."
He mounted and rode toward Semenovsk.

Through the slowly dispersing powder smoke, Napoleon saw horses and men lying in pools of blood, alone or in heaps. Neither Napoleon nor any of his generals had ever seen such horrors or so many killed in such a small area. The roar of guns, which hadn't stopped for ten hours, exhausted the ear and gave a peculiar significance to the scene, like music accompanying a tableau. Napoleon rode up the rise at Semenovsk, and through the smoke saw ranks of men in unfamiliar-colored uniforms. They were Russians.

The Russians stood in solid ranks behind Semenovsk village and its knoll, their guns booming ceaselessly along their line, sending forth clouds of smoke. It was no longer a battle — it was a continuous slaughter, futile for both French and Russians. Napoleon stopped his horse and again fell into the reverie from which Berthier had roused him. He couldn't stop what was going on before him and around him — events supposedly directed by him and dependent on him — and this venture, for the first time, seemed unnecessary and horrible because of its lack of success.

One of the generals rode up and dared to suggest leading the Old Guard into action. Ney and Berthier, standing near Napoleon, exchanged glances and smiled contemptuously at this general's senseless proposal.
Napoleon bowed his head and remained silent for a long time.
"At eight hundred leagues from France, I will not have my Guard destroyed!" he said, and turning his horse, he rode back to Shevardino.
